subject: Multinomial-poisson transform - meaning of fixed precision

messages.author: 87e020c3fd9325fa
messages.subject: Multinomial-poisson transform - meaning of fixed precision
parts:
Hi group,

I have been working with the multinomial poisson transform and found it to be very useful.  However, there is one aspect that I am having a hard time understanding.  In the specification of the "iid" models,  we have something like this:

f(individual, model="iid",    hyper = list(prec = list( initial = log(0.000001),  fixed = TRUE))) +

f(prog2, model="iid", constr = TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(0.001), fixed = TRUE)))

However, I am not certain why fixing the precision is necessary. What would be the effect of setting fixed=FALSE in the above?  

Many thanks,

Tom Bird

messages.author: b453c29749de564d
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Multinomial-poisson transform - meaning of fixed precision
parts:
On Fri, 2014-08-08 at 03:42 -0700, Tom Bird wrote:
> Hi group,
>
>
> I have been working with the multinomial poisson transform and found
> it to be very useful. However, there is one aspect that I am having a
> hard time understanding. In the specification of the "iid" models,
> we have something like this:
>
>
> f(individual, model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list( initial =
> log(0.000001), fixed = TRUE))) +
>
> f(prog2, model="iid", constr = TRUE, hyper = list(prec = list(initial
> = log(0.001), fixed = TRUE)))
>
> However, I am not certain why fixing the precision is necessary. What
> would be the effect of setting fixed=FALSE in the above?

what you need is a uniform distributed intercepts, each for each
'individual', which is the poisson trick. we cannot do uniforms on
-\infty,\infty, so we replace these with Gaussians with small precisions
(or high variances). to avoid this precision to be estimated, we have to
fix it to its initial value = log(prec) = -log(var).

H
